title: Suppression-Contrast Tokens: Evaluating Reverse Layer-Contrast for Secret Elicitation

contributions.purpose: Recover secrets that a language model encodes but refuses to reveal, based on a 'present then suppressed' hypothesis.
contributions.mechanism: Suppression-Contrast Tokens (SCT): rank candidate tokens by a suppression gap = mid-layer log-probability minus final-layer log-probability (logit-lens projections at layer L=32 and N=41 of Gemma-2-9B-IT), reversing DoLa's final-minus-mid direction.
contributions.evaluation: On Taboo/Direct, SCT reaches 5.33% TR@5 vs logit-lens 4.33% (+23.1% relative, +1.0pp absolute).
contributions.domain: AI safety / mechanistic interpretability (secret elicitation from LLM internals)
contributions.source_quote: We propose SCT, a simple method for secret elicitation via reverse layer-contrast that targets the hypothesized 'present then suppressed' pattern.

contributions.purpose: Rigorously test whether reverse layer-contrast actually works, using pre-registered criteria and a negative control.
contributions.mechanism: Pre-register four success criteria (premise support, improvement threshold, direction control, statistical significance) and run a DoLa-direction negative control on Taboo and User Gender benchmarks.
contributions.evaluation: The DoLa-direction control collapses to 0.20% TR@5 vs 4.33% logit lens, confirming the suppression direction carries signal (Criterion 3 passes).
contributions.domain: AI safety / mechanistic interpretability (secret elicitation from LLM internals)
contributions.source_quote: We conduct rigorous evaluation with pre-registered criteria, including a DoLa-direction negative control that validates the suppression direction is informative.

contributions.purpose: Report that the method fails and characterize why.
contributions.mechanism: Evaluate SCT against all four pre-registered criteria and test generalization to binary-attribute (User Gender) secrets.
contributions.evaluation: SCT fails 3 of 4 criteria: premise support only ~9.3% (vs 30% threshold), improvement +1.0pp (below +1.5pp), CIs overlap; and it underperforms logit lens on User Gender (1.20% vs 6.95% TR@5).
contributions.domain: AI safety / mechanistic interpretability (secret elicitation from LLM internals)
contributions.source_quote: We report negative results: SCT fails 3 of 4 pre-registered criteria, with the suppression premise weakly supported (~9.3% vs 30% threshold). These findings inform future research on secret elicitation.

self_declared_provenance.quote: This reverses the direction used by DoLa (Chuang et al., 2023), which contrasts layers to surface factual knowledge that emerges in later processing. We hypothesize that for secret-keeping, the opposite direction--mid-minus-final--should surface tokens that are 'present then suppressed.'

Cywinski et al. (2025) introduce the secret elicitation problem and the Taboo benchmark ... They establish logit lens as a baseline ... Our work extends this line by proposing the suppression hypothesis.

This hypothesis is motivated by related findings in other contexts. DoLa (Chuang et al., 2023) shows that contrasting layers can surface factual knowledge ... CoRect (Ma et al., 2026) identifies 'suppression' phenomena in retrieval-augmented generation ... We propose that secret-keeping may exhibit the opposite pattern.

notes: Explicitly a negative-result paper: SCT fails 3 of 4 pre-registered criteria, the core suppression premise is weakly supported (~9.3% vs 30%), and the method does not generalize to binary-attribute secrets; the authors conclude simple layer-contrast is insufficient.
